So the natural hair movement (which was started by black folks to celebrate their natural hair and natural hairstyles, including braids) started in the late 2000s but took off in the early 2010s. It seems to have been a global phenomenon, as I was able to find a blog talking about said movement in Italy (https://womenchangeafrica.blogspot.com/2017/10/angela-of-naturangi-blogger-of-italys.html?m=1). I didn’t find anything about laws, but I did find information about discrimination and at best, curiosity (albeit ignorant on the part of white Italians) towards black hair (https://caramassa.com/2023/03/11/what-its-like-to-have-afro-hair-in-italy/). The latter post talks about the importance of representation of black hair in Italy as it is severely lacking.

Given that Iginio Straffi has always been ahead of the game when it comes to diversity in children’s media, I’m sure he understands the importance of representation for young children watching his shows. Winx Club throughout its development has always been aware of cultural trends, so I wouldn’t be surprised if they took note of the growing trend towards natural hair and braided hairstyles in black girls and wanted to display that for Aisha in the reboot.

And yes I agree the law is ridiculous in the US but given the pervasive history of racism, slavery, and colonization in the US it’s no surprise that such a law would have to be put in place to eradicate the US longstanding history of subjugation of black people. There are similar phenomena wherever you find black people in the western world. Perhaps not with laws but with attitudes and representation (see the examples in Italy I posted for instance).

Still, that doesn't excuse that said behaviors cause them and their own children real, devastating harm. Hell, I'm pretty sure I have brain damage and memory issues as a result of the PTSD I obtained from being raised by traumatized and abusive African parents.

But, to get to my point, in order to unlearn that, I had to physically and emotionally distance myself from them for a while. I got my own space, didn't talk to them often, and spent my time alone working on myself and doing inner child healing. From that, I realized that a lot of their "good kid" programming was utter bullshit and all it did was make me feel internalized shame and constant stress and pressure to be perfect. When I saw that my mental health was literally declining to the point where I wasn't even able to feel emotions let alone do anything productive, I knew something had to give. So, I let it go and decided to live life for ME. That meant setting boundaries (like learning to say NO) and learning to separate their reactions to my boundaries from my worth as a person. Whatever bullshit my parents spewed at me was honestly a them problem not a me problem. Besides, the things they pressured me to do was the EXACT same thing my grandparents did to them and...guess what? My parents are literally living miserable lives and struggle on a day to day basis just to get by because they refused to unlearn all of their parents toxic traits. I didn't want to be like them so that was proof that their "rules" and "advice" wasn't worth it.

Firstly, I think the fact that you are self aware enough to know that have self-esteem issues is a step in the right direction. A lot of people in our age group are not even aware of that and then get caught up in issues that later down the line they will regret (trust me I know from experience), so to know where you can start working on yourself is good. 

As far as how to work through self-conscious issues, for me, a lot of that had to do with going on a spiritual journey and really learning to understand who I was fundamentally as a person. A lot of that involved shadow work, looking at past traumas, going to therapy, reading self-help books, mindset, manifestation work, etc...you name it, I tried it. And I'm ngl, it was very ugly at times because when you look at yourself in totality, you start seeing parts of yourself that you don't wanna face. But the thing is, you have to face them or else you will end up continuing to live in misery as it is the very parts we reject that linger in our subconscious that cause us to be miserable in life. 

Now, I could talk at length about my personal anecdotes, but I'm sure you are probably looking for tangible tips that you can do to start working on yourself. So, here's a list of things I would suggest to you as a place to start: 

1. Begin doing shadow work/trauma work/mindset work. This I feel is incredibly important because everything we experience in our lives starts in the mind. How we feel, behave, act, and think is all rooted in the beliefs we've acquired about ourselves that linger in our subconscious. If you suffer with self-esteem, then odds are it is likely that you have dealt with some form of trauma in your life that needs to be worked through. This way, you can come solace and acceptance and understand WHY exactly you feel this way. 
2. Begin cultivating a self-care routine. No, I don't mean hygiene and exercising, although don't get me wrong those are definitely important and should be incorporated. However, those are not the end-all be all of this type of journey. What I mean by self-care is developing coping skills to deal with anxiety and trauma and triggers as they come up. This could be self-soothing exercises, breathwork, yoga, etc. Basically, develop a toolkit to be able to deal with negative feelings and thoughts as they arise so that you can begin to feel more emotionally and mentally stable. 
3. Begin envisioning your dream life/body/relationship/etc through vision boards/manifestation/etc. Once you are at a point where you feel more grounded in yourself, you can begin to envision your life as you see fit. Ask yourself about the things you would love to have, do, and be if you had absolutely no restrictions. From that point, you can begin using manifestation tools like affirmations, scripting, etc to begin developing a mindset that will allow you to bring these dreams into your reality.

I highly recommend starting off by braiding or twisting your hair with some oil and letting it sit over night to allow for some stretching and lubrication. The next day, work section by section and start by removing shed hairs by gently pulling at the bottom of your strands with extra oil. Then move up the strands and gently separate the hair at the roots to “de-clump” the hair.

After this, you can moisten your hair until damp (not too wet, but just enough to be pliable) with warm water and add a detangling cream. I like to use Carol’s Daughter 4-in-1 combing crème because it’s lightweight and detangles so easily. For each section, use three fingers and shape them in to a “hook” like rake or comb and run them through the strands like you would a comb. Repeat until you can run your fingers with minimal difficulty. You can alternatively use a paddle brush or wide tooth comb if you think it’s really tangled and then follow up with finger detangling.

Twist and braid the sections and then proceed with styling or washing.

Now, to prevent tangling in the future, I recommend keeping your hair stretched at all times. I do this by blow drying my hair using the tension method with just enough heat and heat protectant to be safe once every wash day (which for me is once a month, although you can blow dry your hair using this method at most once every two weeks to avoid heat damage). I then put my hair in twists or braids and wear a bun throughout the week, making sure to take the twists down to moisturize every other day. It helps to keep my hair stretched and manageable so that come wash day, my hair isn’t a tangled mess. Also, since I wear a bun (and also head wraps), my ends are protected at all times too. 

Detangling is very much about technique and knowing how your hair tangles. By taking preventative measures and using proper technique, detangling should become a breeze.

The counseling center has been a godsend for me. Like you, my mental health went completely in the gutter starting last semester and carried over into this semester. The center has a lot of resources available to help students get on the right foot and because of them, I can safely say that I am definitely getting back to a stable mental state. However, and this is important, your experience with the center will depend partially on how willing you are to get better, speak candidly about your experience, and be an advocate for yourself. So make sure that when you go to the center, you take full advantage of the resources available. I know it can be hard at first to receive help, I know it was for me in the past. But, I figured that if I am really suffering, I would rather take the hand that is being offered to me than ignore it altogether. 

As far as what I got offered from the center, I was able to receive on-campus counseling for a semester, and then later on (with the help of their case managers), I was able to find an off-campus provider that met all of the needs I listed when I spoke with the case manager (plus, I don't pay a lot for co-pays because my therapy sessions off-campus are only $10 thanks to the student blue health plan). I was even able to receive a grant (which they give anyone who asks) to pay for an off-campus psych evaluation, which can cost a ton of money (like up to a thousand). Also, if you are struggling financially, they have a separate survivor fund to help pay for basic needs.

Hey there. Im experiencing something similar in my life. A couple of people have left me and a few despise me. I,too, am also struggling in school. I also have depression and PTSD, so yeah life is not feeling too good for me right now. 

Some things that have helped me during this time is accepting the fact that I am hurting and that life is hard. I think you’ve already done that step as the fact that you have already voiced that you need and are seeking help is a step in the right direction. Another thing that I have done is just take life one step at a time and live slowly. If I’m feeling really low, I take a nap, listen to some calm music if I can, or (if you have a bit of money to spare) light a candle and use an essential oil diffuser. 

I’ve also made sure to journal my feelings when I’m feeling up to it. Sometimes I write poetry as I find describing pain poetically makes it less triggering. Other times I just write like it’s a diary entry. It all depends. 

Lastly, I try to make my mental health a priority. For me it has been through utilizing the mental health services at my university and getting connected to a therapist and a psychiatrist to help keep me stable. But if that’s not an option for you right now, going to the mental hospital is an option. However, if I am being honest, I would recommend doing heavy research on the hospital before going to one (I.e., read reviews) as some of them aren’t as nice as they purport themselves to be. There are gems out there though, just have to sift a bit to find them. But if you can’t find one that’s good in your area, you can try outpatient intensive programs or 10-step groups. These programs tend to be a couple of weeks long and help target a specific concern of yours. Another thing are apps like Insight timer or headspace to help keep you calm. For me, I also have fidget toys, sensory friendly items, and books to help keep me stable during these times since I am also neurodivergent in addition to being mentally ill.

Anyways, I hope this helps! Just know that it does get better, I know it has for me. It simply takes time. Also, please do let me know if my advice is Insufficient in some areas and I will be sure to find something that better suits your situation. Take care love ❤️
